Dilnaz came in about her falling science marks. When I asked if anyone at home could help, she said, "I don't ask them for things." A Monday in July. Sarita's desk lamp flickered and died. She didn't mention it. She studied by the ceiling light, squinting. Her cousin Ishita, staying with them for the summer, noticed. "Tell Chacha. He'll get a new one." Sarita shrugged. "It's fine."

A Friday, two weeks later. With Ishita beside her, Sarita stood at the kitchen door and said, quickly, "Papa, my lamp is broken." Her father looked up. "Since when? Why didn't you say?" That evening he came home with a new lamp. Sarita held it a long time before switching it on.

Sumit, you asked why I never tell anyone what I want, even at thirty. Let me, your Jatin Chacha, tell you something about when I was fifteen.
In our house in Kanpur, we were five children, and money was tight. Every time I asked for anything, a cricket camp, a new school bag, to study art, the answer was “Not now,” or no answer at all. After a while, I stopped asking. I'd think, what's the point?
